findings.title: include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' required by the serializer convention
findings.body: Every other conditional attribute in this file follows the `include_#{attr}?` naming convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, and the dynamically generated `include_#{attr}?` methods from `staff_attributes`/`private_attributes`/`untrusted_attributes`). The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no `?`), so the serializer will never find/call it as the inclusion-guard for the `website_name` attribute. As a result `website_name` is unconditionally included in the serialized output (even as `null` when `website` is blank), ignoring the intended `website.present?` gate. This also means any attempt to hide `website_name` based on trust-level/anonymous rules (see related finding) cannot work even if added, since the guard method itself is never invoked.

findings.title: website_name leaks the restricted website attribute to untrusted/anonymous viewers
findings.body: `website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which hides it from anonymous viewers when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. TL0 users). The new derived attribute `website_name` (lines 137-155) is computed directly from `website` via `object.user_profile.website` but is not added to `untrusted_attributes` and has no equivalent restriction check (its `include_website_name` method only checks `website.present?`, not the trust/anonymous restriction). Consequently, a TL0 user's website hostname (and sometimes the full host+path) will still be exposed to anonymous visitors even though the underlying `website` field is correctly hidden for them, defeating the existing privacy control.

findings.title: No test verifying website_name is restricted for TL0/anonymous viewers like website
findings.body: The 'with a TL0 user seen as anonymous' context (lines 6-16) asserts that `website` and other untrusted attributes are hidden, but does not include `website_name` in `untrusted_attributes` nor set a website on the fabricated user to actually exercise the check. This missing coverage allowed the access-control gap (website_name leaking despite website being restricted) and the broken `include_website_name` guard to go unnoticed.

findings.title: Asymmetric subdomain matching logic in website_name
findings.body: The matching logic handles the case where the Discourse host has an extra subdomain relative to the website host (e.g. website 'example.com' vs instance 'forums.example.com', tested in spec), via `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`. However the reverse case — the website host has an extra subdomain relative to a bare instance domain (e.g. website 'http://forum.example.com' vs instance host 'example.com') — is not handled: the `ends_with?` check is only performed in one direction, so this case falls through without expanding to the full path even though it represents the same underlying domain relationship. This asymmetry is untested and likely not intended given the feature's goal of detecting same-domain websites.

findings.title: Mutating string literal with << instead of safe concatenation
findings.body: `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses the mutating `<<` operator on the string literal `"."` rather than `+` or interpolation. This happens to work today because the file has no `# frozen_string_literal: true` magic comment, but it is fragile: if frozen string literals are enabled for this file in the future (a common Rails convention), this line will raise a `FrozenError` at runtime. It should use `".#{website_host}"` or `"." + website_host` instead.
